title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1984
description:
The first year of 2600, twelve monthly issues beginning in January 1984, when the magazine was a few photocopied sheets of telephone network intelligence edited by Emmanuel Goldstein.

The debut carries "AHOY! - 2600 Debuts" alongside "FBI Goes After ADS Hackers" and "The Truth Behind Those 9999 Numbers." Across the year the newsletter prints a White House phone list, guides to Telenet, MCI and Telemail, MILNET host tables, CN/A and E-Com dialups, and "Arpanet Hopping: America's Newest Pastime." "ESS: Orwell's Prophecy" and "TRW: Big Business is Watching You" state the surveillance argument the magazine has made ever since. Hardware begins with "Introducing the Clear Box!"; "Some Thoughts on 'Garbage Picking'" and "More on Trashing" make dumpster diving a standing subject. Later issues add "The Hacker's Guide To An Area Code," "History of British Phreaking," "Vital Ingredients: Switching Centers and Operators" and "Fun With Fortress Fones."

AT&T's breakup took effect on 1 January 1984, the month 2600 began, and the volume reads as running commentary on it: "The Dark and Tragic Side of the Great Break-up," "Whose Strike Was That Anyway?" and "Be Nice To Your Telco." MCI's lawyers wrote to the magazine before the year was out, an exchange printed as "MCI Mail Targets 2600."
tags: Magazines, Hacking, Phone Phreaking, Computer Security, Surveillance
notes: The twelve 1984 issues are 2600's own reproduction of the first year, sold by the magazine at its HOPE conferences. They are not 1984 printings.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1985
description:
The second year, in which 2600's own bulletin board was seized in a federal raid and the newsletter turned to defending the people it wrote for.

Early issues announce the 2600 Bulletin Board online. By mid-year the headline is "2600 Bulletin Board Seized in Raid on Hackers," printed beside "Sherwood Forest Shut Down by Secret Service" and "The Threat To Us All." Operating systems carry the technical run: "Interesting Things To Do on a DEC-20," a two-part guide to VMS, "RSTS: A Trick or Two" and "Surveying the COSMOS." "The Theory of Blue Boxing" and "What a White Box Can Do" cover the hardware. "The Cipher Disk" is the newsletter's first piece of cryptography, and "A Guide to the Israeli Phone System" starts the foreign-system series. Bill Landreth's Out of the Inner Circle is reviewed, and the year closes with a list of more than 1,500 BBS numbers.

"Some Words on Hacker Morality" and "And They Call US Crooks?" put the ethical case; "Some Important Questions To Ask" is practical advice for readers expecting a visit. "The Infinity Transmitter - An Old Bug" and "The Early Phreak Days" begin the newsletter's habit of writing its own prehistory.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1986
description:
The third year, which opens with the Private Sector board coming back online and closes on cellular telephony, the technology that would occupy the magazine for the next decade.

"Private Sector Returning" leads the year, followed by "Divestiture: What Happened?" two years after the AT&T break-up. Construction and code run throughout: blue box programs, "An Overview of AUTOVON and Silver Boxes," "Mobile Phones - Theory & Construction," "Boxing on ITT" and "Cellular Telephones - How They Work." Systems coverage finishes the VMS series and adds "RSTS For Beginners," "Knowing UNIX," "How To Hack a Pick" and "Violating a Vax." The newsletter also prints "Exploits in Operator Hell," "A Story of Eavesdropping," "The Free Phones of Philly," "Death of a Pay Phone" and "Trashing: America's Source for Information," with number lists for Winnipeg, London and Britain's boards.

Two reviews record how the subject was being written about elsewhere, The Computer Underground and a computer crime review. "The Computel Scoop" opens a story the newsletter finished the following year, and "Things We're Not Supposed To Know About" closes the volume.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1987
description:
The fourth and last monthly year, twelve issues that end with 2600 about to become the quarterly it has been ever since.

"TAP: The Legend is Dead" opens the volume with the end of the newsletter 2600 had succeeded. COSMOS gets a guide and a second article, and Telenet, TSPS and equal access get guides of their own. "Hacking PC Pursuit," "More Vax Tricks," "IBM's VM/CMS System" and "Capturing Passwords" carry the systems coverage. The telephone material widens well beyond North America: "Phoning From Europe," "English Dial-it Service," Saudi Arabian and South African BBS lists, and an AT&T submarine cable map. "The Ballad of Captain Crunch" and an interview with Hugo Cornwall fill out the year. "Cellular Fraud," "How Phreaks are Caught" and "FBI Revealed" run alongside "New York Telephone Exposed."

"Computel Put to Sleep" ends the story begun in 1986. From Spring 1988 the newsletter became a digest-sized quarterly magazine, and the monthly sheets of the first four volumes were never resumed.

"Hacking PC Pursuit," "More Vax Tricks," "IBM's VM/CMS System" and "Capturing Passwords" carry the systems coverage. The telephone material widens well beyond North America: "Phoning From Europe," "English Dial-it Service," Saudi Arabian and South African BBS lists, and an AT&T submarine cable map. "The Ballad of Captain Crunch" and an interview with Hugo Cornwall fill out the year. "Cellular Fraud," "How Phreaks are Caught" and "FBI Revealed" run alongside "New York Telephone Exposed."

"Computel Put to Sleep" ends the story begun in 1986. From Spring 1988 the newsletter became a digest-sized quarterly magazine, and the monthly sheets of the first four volumes were never resumed.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1989
description:
The 1989 volume, which follows the arrest and prosecution of hackers on both sides of the Atlantic while continuing to document the network they worked in.

Spring opens with "Hackers in Jail" and runs "The Wonders of UNIX," "800 & 900 Exchanges" and "Payphones Explained." Summer prints the first half of a guide to PRIMOS, "Scanning For Calls," "Tips on Trashing," "A Sprint Story," "Spanish Phones" and "A Summer Worm," with reviews of the Pirate Radio Directory and the revived TAP. Autumn covers the NYNEX strike, "British Telecom's Guilty Conscience," "The Death of COSMOS?," "The Secrets of 4TEL," REMOBS, voice mail hacking and "Punching Payphones." Winter carries "The AT&T Story," NYNEX central office data, the second half of the PRIMOS guide and instructions for building a silver box.

Autumn's report on the Galactic Hacker Party, held in Amsterdam that August, is the magazine's first coverage of a large European hacker gathering, a connection it kept through the Dutch camps of the following decades.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1990
description:
The 1990 volume, published through the year of the E911 document prosecution and the founding of the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

Spring prints "The 911 Document," the file at the centre of the government's case, next to "How Blue Boxers Are Caught," "Facts About MIZAR," a touch tone decoder project and a review of Clifford Stoll's The Cuckoo's Egg. Summer covers "The Neidorf/Phrack Trial" with an interview with Craig Neidorf and an explanation of the new Electronic Frontier Foundation, under the editorial "A Bittersweet Victory." Autumn turns to Caller ID, with "Defeating Trap Tracing," "The Definitive ANAC Guide," a credit card algorithm and an interview with the cryptographer Dorothy Denning. Winter runs "A Political Hacking Scandal," "The Hacker Reading List," more leaked documents and an anatomy of the 1-900-STOPPER service.

"Fun at the 2600 Meeting" in the Spring issue is an early account of the monthly public meetings the magazine organises, a fixture of its back pages from this period onward.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1991
description:
The 1991 volume, whose Autumn issue printed "Simplex Locks: Illusion of Security," the article that put a mechanical lock among the magazine's cover subjects and drew replies for the next twenty years.

Spring reports the sentencing of Len Rose in "The Terminus of Len Rose," with an Atari virus, a Soviet BBS list, a UNIX password hacker, internet outdials and "The New LEC Order." Summer asks "Where Have All The Hackers Gone?" and covers magnetic stripes, MCIMAX, a tone tracer project, "More on the CLASS Struggle" and a review of Katie Hafner and John Markoff's Cyberpunk. Autumn adds "Dutch Hacker Intrusion," "Protecting Your SSN," "Postal Hacking," "Psychology in the Hacker World" and useful UNIX programs. Winter runs the crypt() source, class features, a COCOT column, mobile frequencies, "Gulf War Printer Virus," "Major Telco Privacy Hole" and "Human Database Centers."

The Simplex piece produced a Simplex and USPS update in the same volume and a full sequel two decades later, "Simplex Locks: Illusion of Security, Version 2.0," in the Winter 2011 issue.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1992
description:
The 1992 volume, in which viruses take up as much space as the telephone network and the magazine reviews both Sneakers and Bruce Sterling's The Hacker Crackdown.

Spring prints an MS-DOS virus, a batch virus, "Virus Scanners Revealed," "Hacking WWIV," "How To Take Apart a Payphone," "The Australian Phone System," "Catching Peepers" and a review of Steve Jackson's Hacker card game. Summer covers portable hacking, a hitchhiker's guide to boxing, a demon dialer review, "Defeating *69," "The View of a Fed" and voice mail hacking. Autumn adds "Hacking AmiExpress," "Defeating Callback Verification," a shopper's guide to COCOTs, a simple C virus and "Toll Fraud." Winter runs "Hackers in a World of Malls," "Cipher Fun," a beginner's guide to Minitel, vehicle identification numbers, a list of Secret Service sites and a letter from prison.

Steve Jackson Games had been raided by the Secret Service two years earlier, which is why a card game gets a technical review here. The Autumn review of The Hacker Crackdown covers the book written about that raid and the prosecutions around it.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1993
description:
The 1993 volume, published while the Secret Service was on trial over the Steve Jackson Games raid and the magazine's attention was moving to cellular telephony and cable.

Spring runs "Cellular Magic," "Trouble in the White House," beige box construction, "Descrambling Cable," "Secret Service on Trial," "A Study of Hackers" and "Getting Your File." Summer prints a guide to the 5ESS switch, "British Credit Holes," "High School Hacking," a DTMF decoder review, meeting advice and a toll fraud device. Autumn covers the Hacking at the End of the Universe camp, "The Wheel Cipher," Caller ID technicalities, "Hacking Honesty Tests," password cracking software, "Changing Your Grades," an overview of DSS1 and a review of Approaching Zero. Winter adds "Hackers in Jail, Part Two," "Cellular Phone Biopsy," "Elementary Switching," "Hacking Smartphone," NYNEX voice mail and digital locks.

Hacking at the End of the Universe, held on a Dutch campsite that August, is the second of the outdoor European gatherings the magazine covered, after the Galactic Hacker Party of 1989.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1994
description:
The 1994 volume, whose Summer issue reports the first Hackers On Planet Earth conference, the New York gathering 2600 organised that August and has run at intervals ever since.

Spring opens with "Crime Waves" and prints a DTMF decoder, NYNEX cards, "Hacking Health," "Software Piracy," facts on the Freedom of Information Act, blue boxing on CCITT System 5, "The Chrome Box" and reviews of Secrets of a Super Hacker and a UNIX security title. Summer covers HOPE itself along with "Life Under GTD5," "The Joys of Voice Mail," "Finger Follies," "Hacking Prodigy," keystroke monitoring and "Detecting Corporate Leaks." Autumn runs "Opening Doors," "Monitoring U.S. Mail," "Irish Telephones," "Hacking Netcash," "Generating an ESN," "The Ten Dollar Red Box" and "Breaking Windows." Winter reports the passage of the Digital Telephony bill and adds "Bypassing Protec," "The Risks of War Dialing," cellular hardware and "Janitor Privileges."

The Secrets of a Super Hacker reviewed in the Spring issue is the Loompanics manual published under the name The Knightmare, a copy of which is shelved in this wing.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1995
description:
The 1995 volume, dominated by two arrests: Kevin Mitnick in February and Ed Cummings, known to readers as Bernie S., a month later.

Spring leads with "The World vs. Kevin Mitnick" and runs "The Gold Card," ATM camera security, cellular interception techniques, "Hacking in Brazil," a 500 exchange guide and a review of Masters of Deception. Summer opens "The Bernie S. Saga" and adds new antiviral technologies, "The Gender Snooper," ATM tricks, "Hacking AS/400," war dialing and a second piece on cable denial. Autumn prints "No More Secrets," stealth trojans, "Military Madness," Macintosh key capturing, a COCOT resource guide, the mutation engine demystified, an ISDN overview and reviews of the films The Net and Hackers. Winter covers "What Happens on the AT&T Side," "A Spoofing Odyssey," "Infiltrating Disney," Ethernet sniffing, Verifone machines and the books The Fugitive Game and Takedown.

Both arrests became long campaigns in the magazine, and coverage of them continued in every volume for the rest of the decade.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1996
description:
The 1996 volume, the year the magazine's subject shifted from dial-up systems to the web, marked by the Spring editorial "Caught in the Web" and the Autumn "PHF Exploit."

Spring runs "Tap Alert," "Unshredding the Evidence," "Confessions of a Beige Boxer," "Hacking Caller ID Boxes," "The Alaskan Phone System," a Motorola cellular guide and "Avoiding Suspicion." Summer covers "Flood Warning," "Scanning Australia," "How To Create Encryption," RCONSOLE hacking, "Flightlink Fun," "Starting a Hacker Scene" and "And Justice For All." Autumn prints "Searches and Arrests," "Hacking the SCC OS," the Brazilian phone system, GTE voice prompts, "Hack Your High School," federal BBS lists, "Building the Cheese Box," "Spoofing Cellular Service" and "The Weird World of AOL." Winter adds "Toward More Secrets," "Chipcards Explained," "Craft Access Terminal," "Cracking AskSam," "Snooping Via MS-Mail," "Social Engineering Via Video" and "Defeating the W95 Screensaver."

"Starting a Hacker Scene" in the Summer issue is an early piece of organising advice. The magazine came back to it in the Summer 2008 issue with "Thirteen Years of Starting a Hacker Scene."

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1997
description:
The 1997 volume, which follows the arrival of GSM and cable modems in North America while the campaign for Kevin Mitnick runs through every issue.

Spring prints "Hacking LED Signs," "Use Your Skills to Escape Boot Camp," "Poor Man's Access," "Consequences of .gov/.mil Hacking," "Credit Card Numbers Via Calculators," cellular programming data, "How To Hack Tech Support," a letter from prison and "How To Legally Use a Red Box." Summer covers cable modem security holes, "GSM Comes to North America," "The Wonders of Net2Phone," "Those Pesky Mylar Strips," "Fortezza: The Next Clipper?," "Tricks and Treats of the Autovon" and "The Ins and Outs of Metrocard Gold." Autumn runs "How To Get Busted by the Feds," "Hacking Fedex," "Brute Forcing the World," "Hacking the Vote," "The EZPass System" and "Secrets of Walmart." Winter adds "The Medical Information Bureau," "TCP/IP Basics and Shortcomings," "The Ominous GETS," "The Potential of Mobil Speedpass," "The Argentinian Phone System" and "Spying on Yahoo."

The MetroCard and E-ZPass articles begin the magazine's long attention to transit fare systems, which runs on through "New York City's MTA Exposed" in 2005 and "Hacking NYC MTA Kiosks" in 2021.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1998
description:
The 1998 volume, whose Autumn issue carries a tutorial on Back Orifice, released by the Cult of the Dead Cow at DEF CON that August.

Spring covers the Defense Switched Network, "More on Military Phones" and "The Mysteries of SIPRnet." It also runs "Eggdropping," "Defeating Cyberpatrol," "A Brief History of Postal Hacking" and "Setting Up UNIX Trapdoors." Summer prints "Where Long Distance Charges Come From," a newbie guide to NT 4.0 and a modem diverter project. "The Tyranny of Project LUCID," "Millenium Payphones" and "How To Hack Your ISP" follow. Autumn adds homemade TCP packets, socket programming, "How To Probe A Remote Network" and "Cushioned Encryption and Deniability." Three articles follow on getting the better of Blockbuster, Moviefone and Radio Shack. Winter runs a touch memory primer, "The Facts of SSN," "Become a Radio Ninja," "Why Anonymous Phone Cards Aren't" and "The Cryptography of Today."

SIPRnet is followed across four volumes, from "The Mysteries of SIPRnet" in this Spring issue to "Still More on Siprnet" in Spring 2000.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1999
description:
The 1999 volume, in which nmap, Netbus and Tripwire arrive in the pages beside the payphone and scanner articles the magazine had been running for fifteen years.

Spring covers vehicle tracking with AVI and ETTM, "Cracking the Time-Banc System," "Wreaking Havoc with Netbus," internet peering, "Fun with Tripwire," "A Hacker's Guide to Getting Busted," an overview of SS7, network scanning with nmap and hacking a Sony PlayStation. Summer prints "Securing Your Linux Box," "Fun at Costco," "Broad Band via the Earth," "Secrets of Copy Protection," two facing articles on parents spying on their children, "The Future of IPV6" and pushbutton lock hacking. Autumn runs "Upload Bombing," "The Terrorist of Orange, Texas," ITS prison phones, "Infiltrating Mediaone," forging ping packets, "Quantum Hacking," Protel COCOTs and an overview of Cellemetry. Winter adds "Accessing Forbidden NTFS Drives," "DATUs - The Tool of the New Age Phreak," "I Own Your Car!," POCSAG and FLEX interception, "Hack The Media" and "Why Redboxing Doesn't Work."

"Why Redboxing Doesn't Work" closes an argument the magazine had run since 1988. "Why Redboxing Still Works (sorta)" answered it four years later.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2000
description:
The 2000 volume, published while 2600 was itself the defendant in the case the major film studios brought over the DVD descrambling code DeCSS.

Spring runs "A Taste of Freedom," "How to Stay a Sysadmin," "Military Computer Secrets," "All About Securid," "AT&T's Gaping Hole," "How PSX Copy Protection Works," "How to Build a Coffee Box" and "How Does That DSS Card Really Work?" Summer covers system profiling, biometrics, "Strange Abuses For Your Home Phone," packet analysis, "Secrets of Dell," "How Domains Are Stolen," Java applet hacking and an interview with Jello Biafra. Autumn, under the editorial "A Summer of Trials," prints "DeCSS in Words," kernel modification with LKMs, "Hunting the Paper Carnivore," anomaly detection systems, "Accessing Federal Court Records" and "Build a Car Computer." Winter adds BellSouth's Mobitex network, Sub7, "Get Anyone's Credit Report For Free," "The DVD Paper Chain," "Hacking an NT Domain from the Desktop" and "Jury Nullification and The Hacker."

Universal City Studios v. Reimerdes was tried in New York that July and decided in August. "DeCSS in Words" and "The DVD Paper Chain" were both written under the injunction that came out of it.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Summer 2000
description:
The 2000 volume, published while 2600 was itself the defendant in the case the major film studios brought over the DVD descrambling code DeCSS.

Spring runs "A Taste of Freedom," "How to Stay a Sysadmin," "Military Computer Secrets," "All About Securid," "AT&T's Gaping Hole," "How PSX Copy Protection Works," "How to Build a Coffee Box" and "How Does That DSS Card Really Work?" Summer covers system profiling, biometrics, "Strange Abuses For Your Home Phone," packet analysis, "Secrets of Dell," "How Domains Are Stolen," Java applet hacking and an interview with Jello Biafra. Autumn, under the editorial "A Summer of Trials," prints "DeCSS in Words," kernel modification with LKMs, "Hunting the Paper Carnivore," anomaly detection systems, "Accessing Federal Court Records" and "Build a Car Computer." Winter adds BellSouth's Mobitex network, Sub7, "Get Anyone's Credit Report For Free," "The DVD Paper Chain," "Hacking an NT Domain from the Desktop" and "Jury Nullification and The Hacker."

Universal City Studios v. Reimerdes was tried in New York that July and decided in August. "DeCSS in Words" and "The DVD Paper Chain" were both written under the injunction that came out of it.
tags: Magazines, Hacking, Phone Phreaking, Computer Security, Surveillance

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2001
description:
The 2001 volume, whose Autumn issue, headed "Consequences," is the magazine's first after 11 September.

Spring prints "Police Searches of Computers," "The Future of PKI" and "Breaking the Windows Script Encoder," with "The Billboard Liberation Front" and "Declawing Your :CueCat." Summer covers "What is Carnivore, Really?" and "Everything Your Parents Told You About ESS was a Lie," alongside pieces on TCP wrappers, password authentication myths and "Snooping the Stack." Autumn runs "Passport Hacking," "How to Decrypt DirecTV," "Code Red 2" and "The Ultimate DRM Hack." It also carries "Defeating Intrusion Detection Systems," an introduction to ARP spoofing and "Hacking Kodak Picture Maker." Winter adds the security of the Inferno OS, "The Future of Enhanced 911," "Building a Floppy Based Router," "Build a Wooden Computer" and "Examining Student Databases."

The CueCat barcode reader, given away free to magazine subscribers that year, is taken apart here and again in Summer 2004 in "Passwords on a Cue Cat."

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2002
description:
The 2002 volume, in which 802.11b wireless networking becomes a subject of its own and the magazine begins tracking the surveillance law passed after 11 September.

Spring runs "Transaction Based Systems," "How to Regain Privacy on the Net," "Stupid Google Tricks" and "The Definitive Guide to Phreak Boxes." "CampusWide Wide Open" and "Defeating Network Address Translation" follow. Summer prints "The Comprehensive Guide to 802.11B Wireless Networks" and "How to Break Through a Proxy or Firewall," with "The Afghan Phone System" and "Getting Into Cisco Routers." Autumn covers "Lawfully Authorized Electronic Surveillance," "The Mysterious World of the Lerg" and "A History of '31337SP34K'," plus a review of Kevin Mitnick's The Art of Deception. Winter adds "Passport Hacking Revisited," "Warspying," "Honeypots: Building the Better Hacker," "Cracking Voter Fraud," "Linux on the Xbox" and "Exposing the Coinstar Network."

The Autumn editorial is "Freedom's Biggest Enemy." Together with "A New Era of Telecommunications Surveillance" in Summer and the Winter piece on the proposed CBDTPA, it sets out the legislative argument the magazine pursued for the decade.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2003
description:
The 2003 volume, published through the invasion of Iraq, opening with the editorial "Not in Our Name" and an article by a hacker sent there.

Spring runs "ANI and Caller ID Spoofing," "A Hacker Goes to Iraq" and "Getting Busted - Military Style," with "Fun with 802.11b at Kroger's" and "Best Buy Insecurities." Summer covers "Traversing the Corporate Firewall," "Staying Anonymous in the Information Age" and hardware key logging. It also prints "Microphones, Laptops, and Supertaps," "McWireless Exposed" and "Why Redboxing Still Works (sorta)." Autumn takes in "Getting to Know Your Neighbors," "Servers on a Ghetto ISP," "Case Mods Made Easy" and "More Xbox Fun and Mischief." "The Hacker Diet" and "The Threat of Biometrics" close the issue. Winter adds "Hacking the Genome," "Living Without an SSN," "WEP: Not For Me," "War Driving with a Pocket PC," "Verizon's Call Intercept" and "Unlocking GSM Handsets."

Wireless runs through the whole volume, from the supermarket article in Spring to three war driving and WEP pieces in Winter, and it is the volume's largest single subject.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2004
description:
The twentieth anniversary volume, opening with the editorial "Twenty Years After" and running the magazine's widest spread yet of articles on ordinary commercial systems.

Spring covers "Taking Advantage of Physical Access," "Hacking the Hilton," "Cruise Cracking" and "Hacking a Mercedes Benz with a Universal Remote." It also runs "Barcode Tricks," "Installing Debian on your Unmodded Xbox" and "Setting Your Music Free: iTunes Music Sans DRM." Summer prints "Scumware, Spyware, Adware, Sneakware," "Impromptu Lock Picks," "Magstripe Interfacing - A Lost Art" and "Passwords on a Cue Cat," with "A Guide to Internet Piracy." Autumn runs "Anti-Forensics: Make Secrets Stay Secret," "Digital CDMA Cloning," "Bit Torrent - The Future of the Internet?," "Hacking Soda Machines" and "Warwalking in Times Square." Winter adds "Hacking CDMA PRLs," "Catching Credit Card Fraud through Steganography," "Hacking LaGard ComboGard Locks," "Hacking Ticketmaster" and "Building Cheap ID Cards."

The Fifth HOPE was held in New York that July, fifth in the conference series 2600 began in 1994.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2005
description:
The 2005 volume, which opens with "New York City's MTA Exposed" and spends the year on Google, voice over IP, and the systems running inside chain stores.

Spring runs "Electronic Application Insecurity," "Voice Over Internet Protocol," "Hacking Cisco IP Phones" and "Hunting Wifi Leeches." It also prints "HP Printers: The Hidden Threat," "Magnetic Stripe Reading" and "Inside the Emergency Alert System." Summer is largely Google: "Hacking Google AdWords," "Hacking Google Map's Satellite Imagery" and "Googlejacking by Example," beside "Home Depot's Lousy Security" and "Spying on the Library." Autumn covers data destruction, "Getting More out of SSH," "Using Tor and SSH Tunneling," "Javascript Injection" and "A Peek Inside a Simple ATM Machine." Winter adds "Hacking a JP1 Remote Control," "The RedBox DVD Kiosk," "How to Track Any UK GSM Mobile Phone" and an introduction to the Asterisk PBX.

Tor appears in the magazine for the first time in the Autumn issue. It became a standing subject: its control protocol in 2009, running a hidden service in 2017, and the disappearance of hidden services in 2021.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2006
description:
The 2006 volume, in which the magazine acquired its named columns and, in the Winter issue, more pages than it had ever run.

Spring covers "Filesharing using TinyURL.com," "XSS'ing MySpace.com," "United Kingdom: The State of Surveillance" and "Hacking the Facebook," with "The Secrets of Cingular Wireless" and "A Look at Jabber/XMPP." Summer adds "More on Hacking Facebook," "Getting Screwed by PayPal," "Easy Access to T-Mobile and Cingular Accounts" and "Breaking Mac OS X Program Security." Autumn runs "Identity Theft: Misinformation Can Be Your Friend," "Where Have The Philes Gone?," "A Back Door to Your Oracle Database" and "Hacking Flickr." "Never Pay for WiFi Again!" and "Attacking Third Party Tracking" close it. Winter covers "Circumventing the DoD's SmartFilter," "Red Boxing Revealed for the New Age," "How to Build a Book Safe" and "The Not-So-Great Firewall of China."

TELECOM INFORMER, HACKER PERSPECTIVE and TECHNO-EXEGESIS all begin here. The HACKER PERSPECTIVE slot, a guest essay in every issue, was filled across the four issues by The Cheshire Catalyst, Bruce Schneier, Mark Abene and Phillip Torrone.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2008
description:
The 2008 volume, which runs a short story in each of its four issues and gives voice over IP, RFID and barcodes the space the magazine had once given to boxes.

Spring covers "Vhreaking with VoxALot," "Dirt-Cheap Phone Calls - The VoIP Way," "Gaming AT&T Mobility," "Hacking Two-Dimensional Barcodes," "Dissecting the EPC: RFID for the Commercial Sector," "Eavesdropping with LD_PRELOAD," "Remember CompUSA," "The EU Directive on Data Retention: Surveillance 2.0" and the story "To Kill an Atomic Subwoofer." Summer prints "Don't 'Locate Me'," "Exploring Road Runner's Internal Network," "The HughesNet FAP," "Hacking Society," "Thirteen Years of Starting a Hacker Scene," "Hacking: A Graffiti Writer's Perspective," "Capturing Botnet Malware Using a Honeypot," "JavaScript Password DOMination" and "The Geek Squad." Autumn runs "Bell's Mind Markup Language," "The TORminator," "The State of Cyberspace and Cyberwar," "Watching the Watchers," "Penetration Testing: The Red Team Way," "Blackhat SEO," "USB Antiforensics" and "Hacking Music." Winter adds an introduction to forensic data recovery, "Social Engineering the Stock Market," "Hack Thyself," "Anonymous SSH at the Library," "Pappy's Cheese Box," "Gaming Gamestop" and "Hacking WebCT."

The Last HOPE was held in New York that July. The year's guest essayists were Martin Eberhard, Barry Wels, Nick Farr and Bre Pettis.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2009
description:
The 2009 volume, which prints a directory of hackerspaces across all four issues as the movement it documents spreads through North America and Europe.

Spring opens with "Year 26" and runs "ATA Security Exposed," "Outsourced," "MP3s: A Covert Means of Distributing Information" and "Inside Google Radio." Autumn prints "Exploiting University Students using Rogue Access Points," "Post-Apocalyptic Communications," "Cracking WPA - PSK" and "Hard Disk Encryption, No Excuses." Winter adds "Pwning Past Whole Disk Encryption," "Hacking Tor's Control Protocol," "Underground Physical Network" and "Retail Automation - ABS."

The HACKER SPACES listings cover North America, Europe, the rest of the world and then new foreign entries, one section an issue. HACKER HAPPENINGS begins in the same volume.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2011
description:
The 2011 volume, published through the year of Anonymous, which the magazine covers twice under near-identical titles and from opposite directions.

Spring runs "Why I Like E-Books," "Who is Anonymous or How to Troll the Media for Fun and Profit" and "How to Accept Payments Anonymously." Autumn prints "Introduction to Chrome OS," "Bypassing Shell Restrictions," "Network Anonymity Through 'MAC Swapping'," "Video Game Hacking" and the story "Kill Switch." Winter adds "Who is Anonymous?," "Free Phone Numbers with Google Voice," "MAC Spoofing Your Way to Free Internet," "Hacking Refog Keylogger," "Pirating the Caribbean" and "The Piracy Situation."

The Winter issue's "Simplex Locks: Illusion of Security, Version 2.0" returns to the Autumn 1991 article of the same name after twenty years. "The Piracy Situation," in the same issue, opened an exchange that filled three articles the following summer.

description:

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2013
description:
The thirtieth volume, published through the summer of the Snowden disclosures, with the Autumn editorial "The Right to Know."

Spring covers "Guest Networks: Protection Less Than WEP?," "Practical Cryptanalysis," "Social Engineering: Tactics for Prevention" and "Extra-Legal Harassment." Summer prints "Splunking the Google Dork," "Fun with the Minuteman III Weapon System," "A Broad Spectrum of DRM" and "0-Day Adventures," beside "Cyber Attacks on Equities Markets." Autumn runs two articles on Bitcoin, "Hacking The Apple Collective," "Internet Trolls," "Access Tandem Codes and the Hidden Phone Network" and "Defeating Forensic Attacks on Full Disk Encryption." Winter adds "Privacy - A New Hope Through Tails," "Wi-Fi Security: Attack and Defense," "Pretty Good Privacy" and "The Growing Schism Between Hackers and the Law."

Bitcoin enters the magazine in the Autumn issue. One article introduces it, and a second asks whether it is the hacker currency, a question the volumes since have kept returning to.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2020
description:
The 2020 volume, whose Spring editorial "The New Social Disease" was written as the pandemic closed the offices its readers worked in.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2021
description:

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2026
description:
The current volume, two issues in, Spring and Summer 2026, the forty-third year of continuous publication.

Spring runs "Trust But Verify: Cross-Checking LLMs," "Anti-Revisionist Malware," "Datacenter Adventures" and "Vibe Hacking." It also prints "Modern BBSing: Scene Update," "The Pirate's Code: From Blackbeard to BitTorrent" and "AI-Powered License Plate Readers Are Ushering a Surveillance State." "Gatekeeping Is Just Bad OpSec," "Salting the NAS" and "Parasitic Computing Like It's 2001" close the issue. Summer covers "HOPE Springs Eternal," "The v6 Network Speaks First" and "Using AI to Generate Code: Verification Coding Is Not Vibe Coding." It adds "Bulletin Board Systems Are Back !," "Playing With ISP Hotspots for Fun and Profit," "How I Escaped From Domain Name Purgatory," "Console Hacking Primer" and "Vibe Coding Kernel Exploits."

Bulletin board systems are a subject in both issues, forty-one years after the newsletter first printed a list of board numbers. "Dr. Hook vs. God's Eye" begins as a two-part serial, and "Neuron Intelligence in Cyber Security Software" concludes.
